misreadings.quote: While his family saw him as a monster, she sees him as a 'nuisance'
misreadings.evidence: she tried to make a nuisance of herself and poked at him a little
misreadings.explanation: In the text the cleaner makes a nuisance of herself by poking him; nobody describes Gregor as a nuisance.

misreadings.quote: to her, he has been demoted from a monster to a mere nuisance
misreadings.evidence: she tried to make a nuisance of herself and poked at him a little
misreadings.explanation: The word 'nuisance' describes the cleaner's own behaviour, not how she sees Gregor, and the text never has her regard him as a monster beforehand.

misreadings.quote: As his shell is shoved across the floor, Grete’s exclamation of 'At last!' rings out
misreadings.evidence: as she turned the key in the lock she said loudly to her parents “At last!”. ... only when she found she could shove him across the floor with no resistance at all did she start to pay attention.
misreadings.explanation: Grete says 'At last!' while Gregor is still alive, when she locks him in the night before; the shoving happens the next morning and is done by the cleaner.

misreadings.quote: not as a sigh of exhaustion, but as a victory cry. Her exorcism is complete
misreadings.evidence: she said loudly to her parents “At last!”
misreadings.explanation: The text gives only the words and that they were said loudly, so calling them a victory cry rather than relief is unsupported certainty.

misreadings.quote: the family moves from stagnant debt to a new, predatory vitality
misreadings.explanation: The text read ends with the cleaner shoving the body; nothing shows the family moving on or becoming predatory.

misreadings.quote: her accusation that he is 'playing the martyr'
misreadings.evidence: She thought he was laying there so still on purpose, playing the martyr; she attributed all possible understanding to him.
misreadings.explanation: The cleaner only thinks this; the text does not show her voicing it as an accusation.

result.note: Most of the reflection is interpretation grounded in the text. The clear errors are the 'nuisance' misattribution, moving Grete's 'At last!' to after the death in the translation, and the unsupported claim about the family's future.
